newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. adds 339,000 jobs in February.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. adds 339,000 jobs in February.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department reported non-farm payrolls rose by 339,000 in February against a downwardly revised 247,000 increase in January.
Economists in a Reuters survey had expected non-farm payrolls to post a 230,000-job gain in February.

WAYNE AYERS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANK OF BOSTON: "It's not a repeat of last February. The numbers were unambigously strong, (but the report is) ... not going to prompt a March move by the (Federal Reserve)."
Ayers was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

KEVIN FLANAGAN, VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "Needless to say, it's stronger than expected. Just about every sector of the report on the surface shows renewed momentum in job creation.

"You're seeing wage pressures developing and the work week came back in a major way. This is definitely going to put the (bond) market on the defensive. I still think the March (Fed) meeting is an unknown. But I think it is safe to say that by Memorial Day, you will have a higher (federal) funds rate."

DAVID SLOAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CONSULTING FIRM I.D.E.A. INC: "This report does not change things dramatically in terms of Fed policy. The payroll growth number was above expectations at 339,000. The main strength was in construction, which the Labor Department tied to mild weather. The hourly earnings data, (up three cents to $12.09 in February) didn't cause much of a scare," he added.
ASTRID ADOLFSON, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH INC: "There were parts that showed good payroll gains, a very long workweek, average hourly earnings up, unemployment rate down.
Adolfson added: "Overall, a very solid report. (Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan has nothing in this report that can stop him if he wants to tighten (monetary policy).
"This report doesn't change my view ... there's still a 75 percent chance they'll go as early as March," she added.

GARY THAYER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, A.G. EDWARDS & SONS INC: "It still shows a big gain in employment and the drop in the (jobless) rate shows the economy is still doing well. We only had a moderate increase in earnings and given the fact that February payrolls are often erratic, I don't think this suggests the Fed is going to (tighten imminently)."

ROBERT DEDERICK, CONSULTING ECONOMIST, NORTHERN TRUST: "The numbers seem to have been exaggerated by the huge surge in construction jobs. It's not a report that seems explosive, but it does suggest the economy is still on a roll and leaves very much open the question of whether it's on too fast a roll. It's a big time number on growth, but there's no big time numbers on inflation. So the Fed is still asking what (is it) going to do. (Policymakers) are looking for something to tell world (a rate hike) is a reasonable thing for the Fed to do. I don't think (a rate hike at the March 25 policy meeting) is a sure thing at all."

DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "Overall the tone of the report is quite strong ... you did have construction giving us an additional boost in jobs. Underlying growth is still very strong, 230,000 service sector jobs -- that's a lot. The risk (of tighter interest rates) is still there. The Fed has identified inflation risk and certainly the stong labor market is going to continue to create a problem for them. But I think there is still some uncertainty as to the transition process, whether this translates into (retail) inflation."
EVELINA TAINER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, INDOSUEZ CARR FUTURES: "There's no question this economy is booming. The chances of them moving on March 25th has increased five fold.

"I wonder if people are going to start talking about a 50 basis point move. It's certainly a possibility given the fact that the next (policy meeeting) is not until May, and if they continue their pattern of moving at meetings, doing 25 (basis points) now and waiting until May is less meaningful than just doing 50 all at once."

JOSEPH LIRO, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CIBC WOOD GUNDY SECURITIES CORP: "The headlines, in terms of the workweek and payroll change, were spectacluar. But when you put it in the context of a modest downward revision to December and January and with an upward bias to construction, the report was not quite as powerful as the headlines would indicate.

"It points to a continuation of solid economic growth in the first quarter with a lot of momentum into the second quarter, with no hard evidence of inflation acceleration. It's not a clear cut call for a tightening at the March meeting."
